topic: Binary Logic in the Towers of Hanoi
target_audience: High school students interested in computer science and discrete mathematics

sections.title: Prerequisite: The Language of Binary
sections.content: Briefly introduce the binary system (base-2). Explain how binary digits (0 and 1) represent positions: the rightmost bit is 2^0, the next is 2^1, etc. Visual: A row of 3 light bulbs turning on/off to represent the numbers 0-7.

sections.title: The Towers of Hanoi Rules
sections.content: Introduce the puzzle: 3 rods and N disks of different sizes. Rules: Only one disk moved at a time, no larger disk can sit on a smaller one. Visual: A 3-disk stack transitioning through states.
sections.example: A monk moving 3 golden disks from Rod A to Rod C.

sections.title: Mapping Binary to Moves
sections.content: The core revelation: The step number (1 to 2^n - 1) in binary reveals which disk to move. Disk 1 (the smallest) moves every odd step; Disk 2 moves every 2 steps; Disk 3 every 4 steps. Visual: A binary counter ticking alongside the movement of the disks.
sections.example: Step 3 (binary 011): The '1' in the 2nd position tells us to move Disk 2.

sections.title: Visualizing the Pattern
sections.content: Demonstrate the synchronization between the binary counter and the disk movement. Highlight that the total number of moves for n disks is 2^n - 1, which corresponds to the binary number consisting of n ones.
sections.example: For 3 disks, the total moves = 2^3 - 1 = 7 steps (binary 111).

sections.title: Real-World Application
sections.content: Conclude by connecting this to recursive algorithms in computing. Binary counting acts as the 'map' for the algorithm to navigate the state space efficiently without backtracking.
sections.example: A robotic arm programmed to solve physical puzzles using an internal binary clock.
